articles.title: California just showed how home batteries will radically remake the grid
articles.content:
Until recently, you’ve had no choice but to be a passive participant in the electrical grid, paying exorbitantly for the juice that flows into your home. But you’re about to play a much more active role — if you’re not already — and get paid to send power from your home battery or electric vehicle to the energy system. Even if you’re a renter, you may be able to buy solar panels that plug into a wall outlet, turning your balcony into your own tiny power plant.

Earlier this month, a punishing California heat wave showed just how this more flexible grid can help absorb spikes in demand. According to the energy-focused nonprofit Common Charge, as the mercury climbed on October 6, home batteries from Tesla and Sunrun provided enough to power every home in San Francisco and San Jose, whose combined population is about 1.8 million, during peak hours.

This sort of adaptability doesn’t just help stabilize the grid, and it doesn’t just compensate the people who supply power — it saves all ratepayers money in the long run. “It also helps the neighbor who doesn’t have solar and batteries,” said Mary Rafferty, executive director of Common Charge. That’s because drawing on energy that’s stored locally is cheaper than building new gas plants or importing electricity from other states when demand outstrips local supply.

That’s the old, rigid way of operating a grid. Historically, a utility has met demand by forecasting when energy use is going to spike, like late afternoons during the summer, when everyone returns home and turns on their AC. By burning fossil fuels like natural gas, a utility could generate more electricity to keep the grid humming without crashing.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Then came solar panels. Early residential adopters produced electricity during the day to power their own homes and sent whatever they didn’t need to the grid. They got paid for this, but only until the sun set.

Then came home batteries. They allow a home to store plentiful solar energy throughout a hot summer day, then send any extra to the grid for others to use. Sunrun says that last year it fulfilled 1,300 of these so-called dispatch events, and has so far done more than 800 this year, often with homeowners none the wiser. “It actually is a very seamless experience,” said Wyatt Semanek, senior director of communications at Sunrun. “They don’t even know when we’re actually dispatching the battery. We always are retaining a certain reserve of charge.”

The goal is to see this system get ever more powerful as ever more home batteries plug into the grid: The greater their number, the less a utility would need to draw from each of them. What’s more, a home with batteries can become an energy “island,” keeping its lights on during an outage.

Batteries are also helping overcome the “intermittancy” of renewables. If utilities relied on solar panels and wind turbines alone, they’d only have juice when the sun shines and the wind blows. Now, though, they’re using battery facilities to store that power and discharge it as needed. “We are able to capture that power through home batteries, through community-scale batteries, and then put clean electrons onto the grid when it’s needed most,” Rafferty said.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

At the same time, utilities are experimenting with tapping EVs, which are basically giant batteries on wheels. This is known as vehicle-to-grid technology, or V2G: Instead of just drawing from the grid, the battery in some models can send power in the other direction. (Sunrun is among several companies that have launched V2G pilot projects.) Consider, for example, an EV owner who drives to work, charges there, then drives back home and plugs in again in the late afternoon. The car has plenty of juice left, so the owner can opt to let the utility take some as demand rises. Then in the middle of the night, once the spike has eased, the car will charge its battery, so it is ready to go in the morning.

All of which is to say: The goal isn’t just getting more backup batteries onto the grid, but smoothing out demand. V2G promises to be especially powerful when used with vehicles like school buses, which have enormous batteries and operate on predictable schedules, giving the utility a good idea of when that power would be available.

Whether it’s with home or EV batteries, these resources are turning owners into critical participants on the grid, relinquishing energy when they don’t need it and the grid desperately does. Sunrun says that between it and Tesla, 1.2 million batteries are installed across the U.S., capable of dispatching 8 gigawatts back to the grid, almost 11 times what was provided during the California heat wave. Then consider that there are 86 million single-family homes in the country.

“If we unleash this technology, both in California and across the country, we can see that we can power our neighborhoods, our communities, our towns, our schools with local power,” Rafferty said. “And if we do that, we are going to be able to keep costs contained, and we are going to be able to provide reliable energy for everybody.”
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant and tangible advancement in energy grid management through home and EV batteries, which helps stabilize the grid during peak demand, reduces reliance on fossil fuels, lowers costs for all ratepayers, and supports renewable energy integration. This has broad societal and environmental benefits, with clear details on how the technology works and its expanding impact.

articles.title: How kites and ancient design are replacing fuel in Antarctic exploration
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The last time a team completed a comparable crossing of Antarctica’s interior, they burned through roughly 170,000 liters (about 45,000 gallons) of fuel to do it. The Wind Sled expedition that left Spain on October 18 plans to use none. Spanish polar explorer Ramón Larramendi is leading four people […]
The post How kites and ancient design are replacing fuel in Antarctic exploration first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

The last time a team completed a comparable crossing of Antarctica’s interior, they burned through roughly 170,000 liters (about 45,000 gallons) of fuel to do it. The Wind Sled expedition that left Spain on October 18 plans to use none.

Spanish polar explorer Ramón Larramendi is leading four people across 3,400 kilometers (about 2,100 miles) of Antarctic interior on a kite-powered platform he has been designing for 25 years, with 16 research projects running the entire way. The vehicle runs on wind and solar energy, meaning no combustion engine at all.

Twenty-five years of design, rooted in Inuit tradition

Larramendi has spent 25 years developing the Wind Sled and has logged more than 28,000 kilometers (about 17,400 miles) across ice on earlier expeditions while refining it. The platform is built on Inuit sled-building techniques, which is an unusual starting point for a cutting-edge scientific research vehicle, and Larramendi doesn’t try to make it sound otherwise.

“The wind sled is something completely unique in the world,” he says. “This sled combines Inuit techniques, which can look like old-fashioned and slightly strange bits of technology. That makes it a very, very unusual mix, but hugely efficient.”

The sled is 15 meters (about 49 feet) long across four modules, capable of carrying up to 2,100 kilograms (about 4,600 pounds). This expedition is running lighter, around 250 kilograms (about 550 pounds) of instruments. The crew has 20 kites ranging from five to 150 square meters (about 54 to 1,615 square feet) in sail area, swapped out as conditions change. The sled can hit 80 kilometers per hour (about 50 miles per hour) in a strong wind; average cruising speed is around 25 (about 15 miles per hour).

Sixteen research projects in terrain that rarely gets visited

The route goes from Russia’s Novolazarevskaya base in Queen Maud Land, through the Pole of Inaccessibility and near the Pole of Cold, finishing at the Concordia research station at Dome C. Five scientific stations will be established along the way. The 16 projects were selected by Spain’s polar research committee, with collaborators including NASA’s Ames Research Center, six Spanish universities, and several national research bodies.

One of the NASA projects is asking whether salt rocks sitting on Antarctica’s surface could harbor microbial life. Sensors embedded in the rocks will measure temperature, humidity, and electrical conductivity to determine whether liquid water could form inside them despite conditions that make that seem impossible. It’s the kind of question that sounds like astrobiology because it basically is.

The Dinglac project will use ground-penetrating radar to map the top 10 meters (about 33 feet) of snow to track how ice layers accumulate and shift. The campaign will also sample for microplastics and chemical pollutants, test for microorganisms and viruses, and run assessments of the European Galileo navigation system.

The location makes all of it harder to get any other way. Satellites and permanent stations have limited reach into this interior. “It is taking place in an area for which there are practically no data,” Larramendi says.

The crew are their own experiment

All four team members are Antarctic veterans: Larramendi; Hilo Moreno, a polar guide and mountain technician; Mariusz Potocki, a researcher at the University of Maine; and Javier Selva, a documentary filmmaker who crossed Antarctica with Larramendi in 2011-2012.

They’re also research subjects. The WindSled Mind project, led by Gabriel G. de la Torre of the University of Cádiz, will monitor the team’s psychological responses, sleep, and social dynamics across the 85 days. The data is meant to inform planning for long-duration space missions, where small crews face confinement and extreme isolation from Earth, conditions the interior of Antarctica replicates about as well as anywhere.

“We are the experiment ourselves,” Larramendi says. “Four people isolated for 85 days in the interior of the Antarctic continent.”

A route designed to be repeated

The point isn’t just to complete this crossing. Each return trip lets researchers compare data across seasons to track real changes in ice, climate, and polar ecosystems over time. “Repeated data collection is absolutely key to tracking variations,” Larramendi says.

When the team arrives at Concordia, they’ll fly out and leave the sled dismantled at the station, ready for the return journey. The fuel comparison says most of what needs saying: the last comparable crossing burned through about 45,000 gallons. This one runs on kites and a design that’s been in development since the 1990s, and when it’s done, the plan is to come back.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

articles.personality_title: Kite-powered sled leads fuel-free Antarctic expedition with science and tradition

articles.personality_title: New enzyme-embedded plastics break down quickly in the ocean
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Plastic pollution in the oceans is a big problem because most plastics take hundreds of years to break down. Many places in the sea don’t have enough microbes to help plastics decompose naturally.

**What happened** – Scientists have created a new type of plastic by adding special enzymes that can break down certain chemical bonds. These plastics are compostable and can biodegrade quickly, even in parts of the ocean where there are few microbes. This discovery was published in the journal Nature on October 21, 2026.

**Impact** – This is important because it means plastic waste could disappear faster in the ocean, helping to reduce pollution that harms marine animals and ecosystems. Unlike regular plastics that stay for a long time, these new plastics break down fully in different marine environments, from shallow coastal waters to the deep sea.

**What’s next step** – Researchers will likely work on making these enzyme plastics more available and affordable for everyday use. If widely adopted, this technology could change how we produce and dispose of plastic, leading to cleaner oceans.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have developed enzyme-enhanced plastics that can rapidly and fully break down in the ocean, offering a new way to fight plastic pollution.

articles.title: In Michigan, 3 tribes are on a mission to bring back a fish that disappeared 100 years ago
articles.content:
This coverage is made possible through a partnership between Grist and Interlochen Public Radio in northern Michigan. ​​

Even when they’re young, the characteristic iridescent hues of the Arctic grayling are noticeable at the right angle.

On a brisk morning in September, fish and wildlife biologist Sean Leask counted and measured hundreds of these fish, which were raised at the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians’ streamside rearing facility, located just outside Traverse City in northern Michigan.

“Some of these might be catchable by the end of next year,” Leask said. “I don’t know what their growth will look like in the wild.”

That’s because Arctic grayling haven’t been seen in Michigan waters for almost a century. By the 1930s, industrial activity like logging and overfishing, along with competition from non-native fish, had decimated their numbers. But three northern Michigan tribes and the state are trying to change that by reintroducing the fish to local waters.

“Our taking care of them and helping them to reestablish their population helps us to reestablish ourselves, our culture, and our traditions,” said Tina Frankenberger, the Grand Traverse Band’s tribal environmental resiliency lead.

Their work joins broader efforts by tribes around the country to restore native species — from salmon to oysters to condors — that are culturally and economically important, while also strengthening the ecosystems that these species depend on against threats like climate change.

One year into raising and releasing grayling to northern Michigan waterways, biologists with the Michigan tribes are grappling with questions about whether the fish are surviving and how to adapt their efforts to extreme weather. No released grayling have been seen in the wild. Flood conditions and the small number of fish they began with are complicating survey work.

But the tribes remain optimistic that their restoration efforts will improve as they collect more data in the coming years. Biologists think it will be around six to eight years before they can tell if grayling reintroduction has been successful.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“This is an experiment,” said Dan Mays, inland policy biologist for the Grand Traverse Band. “We’re trying our best.”

Young Arctic grayling swim in holding tanks at a Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians streamside rearing facility near Traverse City. Vivian La / IPR News

In the summer and early fall, the Grand Traverse Band raised around 8,000 young grayling and released them into the Boardman-Ottaway River. They’re one of three northern Michigan tribes that received grayling eggs from a state hatchery in 2025, along with the Little River Band of Ottawa Indians and the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians. This was the culmination of years of planning plus millions of dollars in combined state, federal, and private funding to restore ecosystems. The eggs for Michigan’s reintroduction efforts were sourced from the Chena River in Alaska, a state where Arctic grayling are plentiful and more genetically diverse than the only remaining population in the Lower 48, in Montana’s Big Hole River.

Mays is already feeling more optimistic about the number and the size of the grayling that the Grand Traverse Band raised compared to last year, when a power outage at the tribe’s rearing facility killed a majority of the grayling.

“Overall, four times as many grayling,” he said. “We’re also stocking a higher proportion of bigger grayling this year. Greater size, greater survival.”

Raising the grayling is one challenge. Tracking the fish to see whether they’ve survived is another. None of the three northern Michigan tribes have recaptured a grayling yet.

“It’s like looking for a needle in a haystack, and the haystack is the size of a river,” said Alex Ontkos, an inland fisheries biologist with the Little River Band of Ottawa Indians. Earlier this year, this tribe stocked 391,000 grayling eggs using in-stream incubators on the Manistee River near Kalkaska. Not all of those eggs hatched, with viability rates estimated around 50 to 60 percent, Ontkos said.

Unlike the Grand Traverse Band, the Little River Band let larvae hatch directly into the incubators, grow into tiny fry, then leave the incubator. While biologists observed tens of thousands of fry leaving the incubators, they have yet to see or recapture a grayling.

“I don’t think that that’s because they’re not out there,” Ontkos said. “It’s just a matter of being in the right place at the right time.” The team with the Little River Band will continue to survey for fish this fall.

Being in the right place at the right time has been trickier for another northern Michigan tribe.

Kris Dey, the hatchery manager for the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians, said two years of ice storms and extreme flooding in parts of northern Michigan have made it hard to tell how fish are surviving or growing, as parts of the watershed are still swollen or blocked by storm debris.

“All the places that we scouted for years and prepped and prepared,” Dey said, “we have not had a great time getting out into the river and evaluating where they’re at and how they’re doing.”

Looking ahead, Dey worries about how a shifting climate might affect grayling restoration efforts beyond worsening extreme weather. The Arctic fish species thrives in cold waters, and Dey said Michigan waterways will likely trend warmer in the future.

“Trying to plan for a warmer future is very, very difficult,” Dey said.

And even after a successful reintroduction, some tribes are grappling with maintaining a species’ stability. Thanks to efforts from the St. Croix Chippewa Indians of Wisconsin, lake sturgeon have made a comeback in the Lake Winnebago watershed, but scientists question whether populations can adapt quickly enough to warming winters.

Staff with the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians wade in the Boardman-Ottaway River near Traverse City, Michigan, to release Arctic grayling.

Vivian La / IPR News

In northern Michigan, biologists said there are ways to adapt their grayling efforts for a changing climate. Dey wants to upgrade the Little Traverse Bay Bands’ current egg incubator system to allow the grayling to grow more before release, in hopes of increasing their likelihood of surviving in the wild.

“Climate change and the dramatic weather that we’re having may make us do things in a different way,” Dey said.

While none of the partner tribes have recaptured a grayling yet, there have been signs of the grayling stocked last year by the team with the Grand Traverse Band. Monitors along the Boardman-Ottaway River have picked up some signals from fish tagged prior to release last year. Leask with the Grand Traverse Band said the signals could’ve been from a brown trout or an otter with a grayling in its stomach, but he wants to be optimistic.

“I’m hopeful they were a live fish with a tag,” Leask said. “It wasn’t many, but enough to give you a little hope.” The tribe plans to do predation studies next year to find out which animals are eating the grayling.

After counting and measuring, staff with the Grand Traverse Band waded out into the north branch of Boardman-Ottaway River with buckets of grayling. Frankenberger sprinkled some tobacco on the water in an Anishinaabe tradition that helps their ancestors hear prayers more clearly, she said.

After saying her prayer, Frankenberger gently tipped the bucket, then watched the grayling slowly disperse downstream in the Boardman-Ottaway River.

“I think about them reestablishing their connection to this river,” she said. “I like to think it’ll help rebuild those connections for our people.”

articles.personality_title: Michigan tribes work to bring back Arctic grayling fish after 100 years
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Arctic grayling fish disappeared from Michigan waters about 100 years ago due to logging, overfishing, and competition from other fish. This fish is important to the local environment and the culture of Michigan’s Native American tribes.

**What happened** – Three Michigan tribes, the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians, the Little River Band of Ottawa Indians, and the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians, have joined with the state to raise and release Arctic grayling back into northern Michigan rivers. In 2025, they received eggs from Alaska, where the fish still live, and have been raising thousands of young grayling to release into the wild.

**Impact** – This effort helps restore a fish species that had vanished, supporting the health of local rivers and reconnecting tribes with their traditions. The project also faces challenges like extreme weather and tracking the fish once released. Although no grayling have been caught in the wild yet, early signs from tagged fish offer hope. The work also shows how tribes are adapting to climate change while restoring nature.

**What's next step** – The tribes will continue releasing more fish, improving their methods to help the grayling survive, and studying how the fish and environment respond. They plan to track the fish better, study what animals might be eating them, and adjust to warming waters. It may take six to eight years to see if the reintroduction truly succeeds.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Three Michigan tribes are working together to bring back a fish lost for a century, blending science and tradition to restore wildlife and cultural connections.

Aunque aún no han capturado ningún pez en la naturaleza, las primeras señales de peces marcados generan esperanza. También muestra cómo las tribus se adaptan al cambio climático mientras restauran la naturaleza.
